fields: IAM's name
replication timing (iam_a.sites.timing)
In the field's terms
Replication timing (Repli-seq): early-, mid- and late-replicating classes
Definition
An input that sorts each molecule into early, mid, or late thirds by the replication timing of its first CpG, built from 15 ENCODE UW Repli-seq tracks.
What it does

It classifies each molecule as early-, mid-, or late-replicating (plain: 'early, mid, late'), giving the instrument a basis for comparing held error across those thirds as ratios within the sample (field_how: held error in early-, mid- and late-replicating regions, as ratios within the sample).
Why the instrument needs it
The instrument's job is to test whether held error depends on when the DNA is copied; this input supplies the timing label each molecule needs before that comparison can be made.
How it is obtained or computed

Derived from 15 ENCODE UW Repli-seq tracks; molecules are split into thirds by the replication timing of each molecule's first CpG. Basis: measured; source: iam_a.sites.timing; source_kind: read from the sample's own molecules.
Where it is read
At each molecule's first CpG, using the 15 ENCODE UW Repli-seq tracks to assign the early/mid/late third.
Where IAM's Law enters

Not part of IAM's Law (law_part: 'not the law itself: a measured input the law uses'; lf_section: 'not part of IAM's Law'). It is a measured timing input the law draws on, not a term within the law's own equation.
Long-form section
not part of IAM's Law
Healthy value and how it is set

Typical/default form: the three-way split (early, mid, late) built from 15 ENCODE UW Repli-seq tracks, sourced as iam_a.sites.timing and read directly from the sample's own molecules (status: measured).

fields: IAM's name
family tracks
In the field's terms
Cell-family-matched replication timing (blood, endothelial, epithelial) — the family track feeding the loss-by-replication-timing instrument
Definition

The record of which cell family — blood, endothelial, or epithelial — a sample's replication-timing data is matched to: the closest family used to read its copy-timing values, read directly from the sample's own molecules via iam_a.sites.timing_by_family.
What it does

It supplies the family-specific timing values (blood, endothelial, epithelial) that instrument 9, Copy timing, uses to check whether held error depends on when DNA is copied, by comparing held error across early-, mid- and late-replicating regions.
Why the instrument needs it

Instrument 9's job is to tell whether held error depends on when DNA is copied; since replication timing differs by cell type, the instrument needs a measured value for the closest family (blood, endothelial, epithelial) rather than treating every sample the same. It is explicitly 'not the law itself: a measured input the law uses.'
How it is obtained or computed
Obtained by measurement: read from the sample's own molecules, drawn from the source iam_a.sites.timing_by_family, yielding the family track blood, endothelial, epithelial.
Where it is read
Early-, mid- and late-replicating regions of the genome, as matched to the closest family among blood, endothelial, epithelial; no single fixed genomic coordinate is given.
Where IAM's Law enters

Not part of IAM's Law — the packet marks its lf_section as 'not part of IAM's Law' and its law_part as 'not the law itself: a measured input the law uses.' It is a measured input quantity feeding the instrument, not a step in the Law's own derivation.

As an input, its value is the family track itself — blood, endothelial, epithelial — sourced from iam_a.sites.timing_by_family and obtained by reading the sample's own molecules (basis: measured); no separate default or healthy band is given for it.

Copy timing by family
In the field's terms
Loss by replication timing: early-, mid- and late-replicating DNA (the late-replicating loss seen with repeated cell division and with age)
Definition
The copy-timing reading repeated with family-specific Repli-seq tracks: held error (and gain error) in early-, mid- and late-replicating DNA, as ratios within the sample, by cell family (e.g. blood).
What it does
It tests whether held error depends on when the DNA is copied, by comparing held error in early-, mid- and late-replicating regions as ratios within the sample.
Why the instrument needs it
The instrument's job is to determine whether held error depends on when the DNA is copied.
How it is obtained or computed

Held error (and related held_iso, held_opp, gain_iso, gain_opp values) is worked out for early-, mid- and late-replicating regions, as ratios within the sample; it is computed by the chain from the sample's molecules and its references, recorded at test path iam_a.sites.timing_by_family (test_state: OK).
Where it is read
Early-, mid- and late-replicating regions, using the Repli-seq tracks of the sample's cell family (the test output is keyed by family, e.g. blood, then early/mid/late).
Where IAM's Law enters

Not part of IAM's Law: law_part marks it as 'not the law itself: a measured input the law uses', and lf_section is 'not part of IAM's Law'. It is a measured quantity the Law draws on, not a step within the Law itself.

Healthy value and how it is set

outputs.name: Copy timing by family

fields: How it works

Held error in early-, mid- and late-replicating DNA (thirds by each molecule's first CpG on 15 ENCODE UW Repli-seq tracks, also by blood, endothelial and epithelial family tracks), as ratios within the sample.
Why
Late-replicating DNA is restored with less time before the next division and loses marks first with repeated division and age; ratios within the sample tare themselves.
Physics
Not the law itself: a measured input the law uses: the time a restore has before the copy is copied again.
Where the data comes from

The sample's molecules; 15 ENCODE UW Repli-seq tracks (ENCODE, University of Washington; Hansen R.S. et al. 2010, Sequencing newly replicated DNA reveals widespread plasticity in human replication timing, PNAS 107:139-144, doi 10.1073/pnas.0912402107) and family tracks.
The numbers
Healthy test library: late slightly above early. Relay test: planted late-replicating loss moved late/early 1.047 -> 1.174 (met).
Method and standard
Counted held error per timing third; ratios within the sample; healthy bar from held-out libraries (owed).
Known-answer test
Relay test (2026-11-20): planted late-replicating loss moved late/early 1.047 -> 1.174 and no other instrument (met).
Limits
(1) Timing tracks come from cell lines, not each atlas type. (2) No measured healthy bar yet.
Where the result goes
bundle iam_a.count timing fields; report.
Code
stage_q2_selfref counter (timing thirds)
How to rebuild it
1. Assign each molecule to early, mid or late by its first CpG on the Repli-seq tracks. 2. Held error per third. 3. Ratios to early.
History
Dated entries in the development log (METHYLPHYS_DEVELOPMENT_LOG.md) and the instrument's development record.
records.name: Copy timing: held error by replication timing (early, mid, late)
questions: Why would late-replicating DNA lose more?
It is copied last, so its marks have the least time to be restored before the next division; late-replicating loss with age is reported in the field.
How exactly is a region classified as early-, mid-, or late-replicating in this analysis?

Each molecule is assigned based on its first CpG site, and regions are split into thirds (early, mid, late) using 15 ENCODE UW Repli-seq tracks. The same split is also done separately using blood, endothelial, and epithelial family tracks.
instrument record: field_how and the rule description describing thirds by each molecule's first CpG on 15 ENCODE UW Repli-seq tracks, also by family tracks
Do the replication-timing tracks actually come from the same tissue as the samples being tested?
No. The replication-timing tracks come from cell lines, not from each atlas tissue type, and the records state this mismatch as a limit of the instrument.
instrument record: rule limits, point (1) on timing tracks coming from cell lines, not each atlas type
What counts as a normal, healthy result for this measure, and is that based on real data?

The expected healthy pattern is 'late slightly higher' than early or mid replicating regions, and this is described as being on a measured basis. However, no measured healthy baseline has been recorded yet, so this expected pattern isn't yet backed by a confirmed reference bar.
instrument record: outputs healthy_how fields and rule limits, point (2) on no measured healthy bar yet
Why does the method use ratios within each sample instead of absolute error counts?
Ratios within the sample are self-normalizing ('tare themselves'), which avoids needing an external calibration and controls for sample-to-sample differences.
instrument record: rule 'why' field describing ratios within the sample tareing themselves
